claim: Steroid hormones are lipid-soluble molecules derived from dietary cholesterol that easily penetrate the brain.
source: These lipid-soluble molecules derived from dietary cholesterol easily penetrate the brain and act through nuclear hormone receptors (NHRs) that function as transcription factors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about steroid hormone properties.

claim: The ecdysone receptor (EcR) and Eip75B (E75) act in glia to regulate the rhythm and amount of sleep in Drosophila.
source: we knocked down each of the 18 highly conserved NHRs found in Drosophila adults and report that the ecdysone receptor (EcR) and its direct downstream NHR Eip75B (E75) act in glia to regulate the rhythm and amount of sleep.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the systematic knockdown screen described in the manuscript.

claim: Ecdysone synthesis genes have little to no expression in the fly brain.
source: Given that ecdysone synthesis genes have little to no expression in the fly brain, ecdysone appears to act as a long-distance signal
evidence: This is supported by reference to single-cell sequencing data mentioned in the manuscript.

claim: Ecdysone enters the brain more at night.
source: ecdysone appears to act as a long-distance signal and our data suggest that it enters the brain more at night.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing differential E75 response to ecdysone injection at different times.

claim: EcR localizes to cortex glia in the brain.
source: Anti-EcR staining localizes to the cortex glia in the brain
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4.

claim: EcR functions in adult cortex glia to affect sleep.
source: functional screening of glial subtypes revealed that EcR functions in adult cortex glia to affect sleep.
evidence: This is based on genetic manipulation experiments using subglial drivers.

claim: Cortex glia are implicated in lipid metabolism.
source: Cortex glia are implicated in lipid metabolism, which appears to be relevant for actions of ecdysone
evidence: This is supported by literature and the experimental findings in this study.

claim: Ecdysone treatment mobilizes lipid droplets.
source: ecdysone treatment mobilizes lipid droplets (LDs)
evidence: This is demonstrated by BODIPY staining experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Knockdown of glial EcR results in more lipid droplets.
source: knockdown of glial EcR results in more LDs.
evidence: This is shown by BODIPY staining in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sleep-promoting effects of exogenous ecdysone are diminished in lsd-2 mutant flies.
source: sleep-promoting effects of exogenous ecdysone are diminished in lsd-2 mutant flies, which are lean and deficient in lipid accumulation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral experiments shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Ecdysone is a systemic secreted factor that modulates sleep by stimulating lipid metabolism in cortex glia.
source: We propose that ecdysone is a systemic secreted factor that modulates sleep by stimulating lipid metabolism in cortex glia.
evidence: This is the main conclusion synthesized from multiple experimental findings.

claim: Sleep is broadly conserved in animals.
source: Sleep is a resting state that alternates with awake and is broadly conserved in animals (Anafi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Anafi et al., 2018.

claim: Loss of sleep has systemic effects and is associated with molecular changes in the periphery.
source: Loss of sleep has systemic effects and is associated with molecular changes in the periphery (Anafi et al., 2013; Chua et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Anafi et al., 2013 and Chua et al., 2015.

claim: Circulating steroid hormones are lipophilic and can easily enter the brain.
source: Given that circulating steroid hormones are lipophilic and can easily enter the brain, together with the broad expression of NHRs in the central nervous system, it is reasonable to infer that NHR signaling is a significant contributor to brain function (Yang et al., 2007; King-Jones and Thummel, 2005; Kininis and Kraus, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2007; King-Jones and Thummel, 2005; Kininis and Kraus, 2008.

claim: Nearly half of known NHRs are highly expressed in adult fly brain both neurons and glia.
source: Based upon single-cell RNAseq data showing that nearly half of known NHRs are highly expressed in adult fly brain both neurons and glia
evidence: This is based on single-cell RNAseq data cited from Davie et al., 2018.

claim: Knockdown of most NHRs in neurons and glial cells reduced adult sleep compared with controls.
source: we found that knockdown of most NHRs in neurons and glial cells reduced adult sleep by varying levels compared with their GS controls and UAS controls, suggesting that the endocrine system in general plays a positive role in sleep regulation
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B,C from the systematic screen.

claim: Knockdown of EcR and E75 had the greatest effects on total sleep among all NHRs tested.
source: Among them, knockdown of EcR, the receptor of the primary steroid hormone ecdysone, and its direct downstream targeting gene Eip75B (E75) had the greatest effects on total sleep.
evidence: This is evident from the screening data shown in Figure 1.

claim: EcR and E75 knockdown affect primarily nighttime sleep.
source: Importantly, EcR and E75 knockdown affect primarily nighttime sleep and phenotypes are stronger when they are knocked down in glia.
evidence: This is shown in the sleep analysis data in Figure 1 and Figure 2.

claim: Flies with glial knockdown of EcR slept on average ~460 min, much less than those with neuronal knockdown that slept ~707 min.
source: Across multiple experiments, we found that flies with glial knockdown of EcR slept on average ~460 min, much less than those with neuronal knockdown that slept ~707 min.
evidence: This is quantified from multiple experiments shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: The total sleep amount of nSyb-GS>EcR RNAi flies was not significantly reduced compared with nSyb-GS control flies.
source: In addition, the total sleep amount of nSyb-GS>EcR RNAi flies was not significantly reduced compared with nSyb-GS control flies, suggesting that glial EcR has a larger role in determining sleep amount
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Knockdown of E75 in either neurons or glia led to severe sleep loss, with ~419 and ~461 min of daily sleep, respectively.
source: Knockdown of E75 in either neurons or glia led to severe sleep loss, with ~419 and ~461 min of daily sleep, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: Ecdysone directly or indirectly affects multiple NHRs.
source: Because ecdysone is the most common steroid hormone in Drosophila, it directly or indirectly affects multiple NHRs (King-Jones and Thummel, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to King-Jones and Thummel, 2005.

claim: Knockdown of ecdysone responsive NHRs reduced sleep more than knockdown of non-ecdysone responsive NHRs.
source: Indeed, we found that knockdown of ecdysone responsive NHRs reduced sleep more than knockdown of non-ecdysone responsive NHRs
evidence: This is based on analysis of the screening data.

claim: Two out of three top hits with neuronal knockdown and five out of seven top hits with glial knockdown are ecdysone relevant NHRs.
source: If we use 200-min sleep loss compared with both control groups as a cutoff, then two out of three top hits with neuronal knockdown and five out of seven top hits with glial knockdown are ecdysone relevant NHRs.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of the screening data.

claim: Genes showing the most dramatic sleep loss when knocked down in glia were EcR, E75, Ftz-f1, and Hr3, all directly relevant to the ecdysone signaling pathway.
source: Genes showing the most dramatic sleep loss when knocked down in glia were EcR, E75, Ftz-f1, and Hr3, all directly relevant to the ecdysone signaling pathway.
evidence: This is based on the screening results shown in Figure 1.

claim: Neuronal, but not glial, knockdown of Hr51 (unfulfilled) resulted in an arrhythmic phenotype.
source: We found that neuronal, but not glial, knockdown of Hr51 (unfulfilled), previously shown to exert circadian effects by acting in central clock neurons (Beuchle et al., 2012), resulted in an arrhythmic phenotype, with no sleep amount change under 12:12 hr light:dark conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D and supported by citation to Beuchle et al., 2012.

claim: Neuronal or glial-specific knockdown of EcR or E75 reduces sleep amount by fragmenting sleep.
source: Sleep architecture analysis showed that neuronal or glial-specific knockdown of EcR or E75 reduces sleep amount by fragmenting sleep, with larger effects seen with the glial-specific knockdown (Figure 2E–H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E–H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–H.

claim: Glial EcR and E75 knockdown flies had shorter average sleep bout lengths during the day and night and more sleep bouts at night.
source: Glial EcR and E75 knockdown flies had shorter average sleep bout lengths during the day and night and more sleep bouts at night, indicating that their sleep is fragmented (Figure 2F, H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F, H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F, H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F, H.

claim: Adult-specific knockdown of EcR is sufficient to reduce sleep in both neuronal and glial populations.
source: Comparison of RU486-treated flies with vehicle-treated controls confirmed that adult-specific knockdown of EcR is sufficient to reduce sleep in both neuronal and glial populations (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E–H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E–H using the GeneSwitch system.

claim: Repo-Gal4; TubGal80ts>EcR RNAi #1 flies sleep a similar amount at permissive temperature (18 degrees) as control flies, but their sleep is significantly less at restricted temperature (31 degrees).
source: The results show that Repo-Gal4; TubGal80ts>EcR RNAi #1 flies sleep a similar amount at permissive temperature (18 degrees) as control flies, but their sleep is significantly less at restricted temperature (31 degrees), confirming that EcR acts in adult glia to regulate daily sleep (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B using the TARGET system.

claim: Three other EcR RNAi lines tested with Repo-GS all produced reduced sleep phenotypes.
source: we also tested three other EcR RNAi lines with Repo-GS, all of which produced reduced sleep phenotypes, further confirming that EcR RNAi knockdown in glial cells reduces sleep (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C–E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C–E.

claim: Glial knockdown of EcI reduced overall sleep levels and led to more fragmented sleep.
source: As with EcR, glial knockdown of EcI reduced overall sleep levels and led to more fragmented sleep (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–D.

claim: In constant darkness, half of the nSyb-GS EcR knockdown flies and 90% of Repo-GS EcR knockdown flies became arrhythmic.
source: In DD, half of the nSyb-GS EcR knockdown flies and 90% of Repo-GS EcR knockdown flies became arrhythmic, but the remaining rhythmic flies showed no difference from controls in their period or FFT (Fast Fourier Transform) values that are a measure of rhythm strength (Figure 2I–K).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2I–K.

claim: EcR functions are required in glia to promote circadian locomotor rhythms and sleep.
source: Our finding that EcR functions are required in glia to promote circadian locomotor rhythms and sleep is novel and consistent with previous work showing that E75 or EcR knockdown in central clock cells causes some locomotor arrhythmicity, but more dramatic phenotypes result from knockdown with drivers such as tim27-Gal4 that additionally express in glia (Kumar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the data and citation to Kumar et al., 2014.

claim: Overexpression of EcR in neurons and glia had no effect on total sleep.
source: Next, we overexpressed EcR and found that, in contrast to our knockdown experiments, overexpression in neurons and glia had no effect on total sleep
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4E–H.

claim: Repo-GS>EcR_c flies showed a consistent phase shift at dusk.
source: overexpression in neurons and glia had no effect on total sleep, but Repo-GS>EcR_c flies showed a consistent phase shift at dusk (Figure 2—figure supplement 4E–H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4E–H.

claim: Effects of EcR on sleep and rhythms are largely through glia, and not neurons.
source: Thus, effects of EcR on sleep and rhythms are largely through glia, and not neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative effects of neuronal vs. glial manipulations.

claim: Starvation raises ecdysone levels in female flies.
source: Starvation is an example of a stressor that raises ecdysone levels in female flies (Terashima et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Terashima et al., 2005.

claim: Feeding of exogenous 20E promotes sleep in fed wild-type flies.
source: As shown by Ishimoto and Kitamoto, 2010 , we also found that feeding of the exogenous bioactive form of ecdysone, 20E, promotes sleep in fed wild-type flies (Figure 3 A, E)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A, E and supported by citation to Ishimoto and Kitamoto, 2010.

claim: Exogenous ecdysone abrogated sleep loss caused by starvation.
source: Exogenous ecdysone abrogated sleep loss caused by starvation, indicating that EcRs are functional in sleep-relevant cells under these conditions (Figure 3B, E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B, E.

claim: mRNA levels of ecdysone responsive genes—EcR, EcI, E75, and E74—in the fly brain are not altered after 1 day of starvation.
source: Consistent with this, we found that mRNA levels of ecdysone responsive genes—EcR, EcI, E75, and E74—in the fly brain are not altered after 1 day of starvation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Starved flies fed 20E showed rebound sleep when they were returned to food.
source: Interestingly, starved flies fed 20E showed rebound sleep when they were returned to food, even though these flies did not lose sleep during starvation, indicating that 20E does not rescue the need for sleep that builds up during starvation (Regalado et al., 2017).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data and supported by citation to Regalado et al., 2017.

claim: Sleep increased following 20E administration in nSyb-GS>EcR RNAi flies, but not Repo-GS>EcR RNAi flies.
source: Sleep increased following 20E administration in nSyb-GS>EcR RNAi flies, but not Repo-GS>EcR RNAi flies (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Neuronal ecdysone signaling appears to be dispensable for sleep-promoting effects of exogenous ecdysone.
source: However, neuronal ecdysone signaling appears to be dispensable for this purpose.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that neuronal EcR knockdown does not block 20E effects.

claim: Robust sleep loss was seen with starvation when EcR was knockdown in glia even though baseline sleep is already quite low in these flies.
source: On the other hand, robust sleep loss was seen with starvation when EcR was knockdown in glia even though baseline sleep is already quite low in these flies (Figure 3D, E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D, E.

claim: Starvation and ecdysone signaling in glia independently regulate sleep.
source: These data indicate that starvation and ecdysone signaling in glia independently regulate sleep and a large part of sleep remaining in starved flies derives from ecdysone signaling in glia.
evidence: This is inferred from the additive effects of starvation and EcR knockdown.

claim: Sleep induced by heat shock was not affected by EcR knockdown in neurons or glia.
source: We also examined the response to a stressor that increases sleep, heat shock, and found that sleep induced by heat shock was not affected by EcR knockdown in neurons or glia (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 20E level is significantly higher at ZT14 than ZT2 in the fly periphery but not in the fly brain.
source: However, ELISA analysis indicated that 20E level is significantly higher at ZT14 than ZT2 in the fly periphery but not in the fly brain (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A using ELISA.

claim: mRNA levels of ecdysone responsive E75 isoforms cycle with a peak at ZT12 in the fly head.
source: In support of circadian regulation of ecdysone signaling, mRNA levels of ecdysone responsive E75 isoforms cycle with a peak at ZT12 in the fly head, suggesting that ecdysone acts rhythmically in the fly brain (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B by qPCR.

claim: E75 isoforms do not peak at ZT12 in the fly periphery.
source: Given that E75 isoforms do not peak at ZT12 in the fly periphery, we suggest that elevated ecdysone at this time enters the brain instead of acting on peripheral tissues.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The mRNA levels of both E75A and E75B increased more at ZT18, compared to ZT6, after 20E injection.
source: We normalized the change in E75 expression in the brain to the change in the body to account for inconsistency of injection and found that the mRNA levels of both E75A and E75B increased more at ZT18, compared to ZT6, after 20E injection, E75A increased 1.67-fold at ZT6, and 3.91 at ZT18, while E75B increased 17-fold at ZT6, and 51.92-fold at ZT18 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Peripheral ecdysone has higher action in the brain at night.
source: This result indicates that peripheral ecdysone has higher action in the brain at night.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential E75 response to 20E injection at different times.

claim: EcR is broadly expressed in the adult fly brain, but largely in the cortex glia.
source: Consistent with previous reports, antibody staining in the adult fly brain showed that EcR is broadly expressed, but largely in the cortex glia.
evidence: This is shown by immunohistochemistry in Figure 4A,B.

claim: EcR antibody staining was greatly diminished when EcR was knocked down in glia with Repo-GS.
source: When EcR was knocked down in glia with Repo-GS, EcR antibody staining was greatly diminished.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: EcR expression signals were preserved when EcR was knocked down in neurons.
source: However, signals were preserved when EcR was knocked down in neurons, leading us to infer that glia, in particular cortex glia, are the major site of expression (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: EcR expression was also detected in surface glia of the blood–brain barrier.
source: Although not evident in these images, EcR expression was also detected in surface glia of the blood–brain barrier (BBB) (data not shown).
evidence: This is mentioned but data not shown in the figures.

claim: EcR knockdown with most subglial Gal4 lines caused failure of eclosion.
source: However, EcR knockdown with most of these Gal4 lines caused failure of eclosion, indicating the importance of EcR in glial cells during development.
evidence: This is an observation from the genetic experiments.

claim: Three Gal4 lines produced viable adult flies: GMR77A03 (cortex glia), Eaat-1 (astrocyte-like glia), and GMR56F03 (ensheathing glia).
source: Three Gal4 lines produced viable adult flies: one cortex glia-specific driver GMR77A03, one astrocyte-like glia-specific driver Eaat-1, and one ensheathing glia-specific driver GMR56F03.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: Sleep was only reduced when EcR was knocked down using the cortex glia-specific driver GMR77A03.
source: Of these three Gal4 lines, sleep was only reduced when EcR was knocked down using the cortex glia-specific driver (Figure 5A, C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A, C.

claim: Sleep decreased significantly at the restrictive temperature when RNAi expression was activated to knock down EcR in cortex glia using NP2222-Gal4/tubulinGal80ts.
source: At the (permissive) low temperature, when TUB-GAL80ts blocks Gal4 expression, flies expressing EcR RNAi flies with the cortex glia driver NP2222 trended toward reduced sleep but sleep decreased significantly at the restrictive temperature when RNAi expression was activated to knock down EcR in cortex glia (Figure 5E, G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E, G using the TARGET system.

claim: Knockdown of EcR with the 9-137 Gal4 driver, which targets all glia of the BBB, did not affect sleep.
source: Knockdown of EcR with the 9-137 Gal4 driver, which targets all glia of the BBB, did not affect sleep (Figure 5F, H)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F, H.

claim: Knockdown of EcR in ensheathing or astrocyte glia did not affect sleep.
source: and nor did knockdown of EcR in ensheathing or astrocyte glia (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that effects of EcR on sleep are restricted to specific glia, with cortex glia being the primary physiological site of action.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only flies expressing EcR with the 9-137 Gal4 driver had elevated sleep when EcR was overexpressed using subglia drivers.
source: We also overexpressed EcR using the same set of subglia drivers and found that only flies expressing EcR with the 9-137 Gal4 driver had elevated sleep (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Flies overexpressing EcR with 9-137 Gal4 were resistant to sleep deprivation, indicating enhanced sleep need.
source: These flies were also resistant to sleep deprivation, indicating enhanced sleep need.
evidence: This is mentioned in the results but specific data not shown in main figures.

claim: Restricting EcR overexpression to the adult stage with TubGal80 did not affect sleep.
source: Restricting overexpression to the adult stage with TubGal80 did not affect sleep, suggesting that the sleep-promoting effect observed in 9-137 Gal4 flies is developmental (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The cortex glia, especially the superficial cortex glial cells, are enriched in lipid droplets in the third instar larval stage.
source: The cortex glia, especially the superficial cortex glial cells, are enriched in lipid droplets (LDs) in the third instar larval stage, and ecdysone signaling can mobilize these lipids when needed (Kis et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kis et al., 2015.

claim: LDs accumulate mostly in the cortex and ensheathing glia.
source: We measured LDs in the fly brain by BODIPY staining and found that LDs, which accumulate mostly in the cortex and ensheathing glia, were significantly smaller in flies fed ecdysone, relative to control groups, at Zeitgeber Time (ZT)12.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A–D.

claim: LDs were significantly smaller in flies fed ecdysone at ZT12, while the total count was not affected.
source: We measured LDs in the fly brain by BODIPY staining and found that LDs, which accumulate mostly in the cortex and ensheathing glia, were significantly smaller in flies fed ecdysone, relative to control groups, at Zeitgeber Time (ZT)12. At the same time, the total count was not affected (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A–D.

claim: EcR knockdown in glial cells resulted in more LDs.
source: We performed lipid staining, comparing vehicle controls and RU486-induced groups of Repo-GS>EcR RNAi flies (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D), and found that EcR knockdown in glial cells resulted in more LDs
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: Ecdysone signaling bidirectionally affects LDs in glial cells.
source: RU treatment of UAS control flies had no effect, together suggesting that ecdysone signaling bidirectionally affects LDs in glial cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the opposite effects of ecdysone feeding and EcR knockdown on LDs.

claim: Ecdysone does not promote sleep in lsd2 mutants.
source: We found that ecdysone does not promote sleep in lsd2 mutants (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Feeding lsd-2 mutant flies gaboxadol, a GABA agonist, significantly increased sleep.
source: However, feeding lsd-2 mutant flies gaboxadol, a GABA agonist known to induce deep sleep, significantly increased sleep (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), indicating that non-responsiveness to ecdysone was not due to an inability of lsd-2 flies to respond to sleep-promoting interventions.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ecdysone affects sleep in large part by modulating LDs in glial cells, especially cortex glia.
source: Lack of a sleep-promoting effect of ecdysone on lsd-2 mutants, together with bidirectional effects of ecdysone on LDs, indicate strongly that ecdysone affects sleep in large part by modulating LDs in glial cells, especially cortex glia (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including lsd-2 mutant response and LD measurements.

claim: Glia are a major target of steroid hormone signaling to regulate sleep.
source: We show here that glia are also a major target of steroid hormone signaling to regulate sleep.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the study.

claim: Ecdysone is the major steroid hormone in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, ecdysone is the major steroid hormone, and it plays an essential role in regulating metamorphosis and molting (Yamanaka et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yamanaka et al., 2013.

claim: Ecdysone affects the development of the nervous system and neuronal remodeling.
source: Ecdysone also affects the development of the nervous system and neuronal remodeling, processes that may involve glial function (Yu and Schuldiner, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yu and Schuldiner, 2014.

claim: During development, ecdysone is synthesized from dietary cholesterol in the prothoracic gland and in other peripheral tissues.
source: During development, ecdysone is synthesized from dietary cholesterol in the prothoracic gland and in other peripheral tissues that control molting and eclosion in larvae and pupae, but it declines during pupa-adult transitions and remains low in adults (Yamanaka et al., 2013; Kannangara et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yamanaka et al., 2013 and Kannangara et al., 2021.

claim: Ecdysone is implicated in adult functions such as memory formation and stress resistance.
source: Nevertheless, it is implicated in adult functions such as memory formation and stress resistance (Ishimoto and Kitamoto, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ishimoto and Kitamoto, 2011.

claim: Ecdysone controls developmental transitions in response to nutrient signals.
source: Our finding that ecdysone regulates sleep through metabolic mechanisms in glia is consistent with other metabolic functions attributed to it; for instance, it controls developmental transitions in response to nutrient signals (Christensen et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2000; Uyehara and McKay, 2019; Xu et al., 2020; Yamanaka et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Ecdysone may affect the whole-body lipid profile to modulate physiology and behavior.
source: Indeed, ecdysone may affect the whole-body lipid profile to modulate physiology and behavior (Sieber and Spradling, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sieber and Spradling, 2015.

claim: The gonads, in particular the ovaries in females, are thought to be the major source of ecdysone in adults.
source: The gonads, in particular the ovaries in females, are thought to be the major source of the ecdysone in adults (Ahmed et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ahmed et al., 2020.

claim: Several peripheral tissues express ecdysone biosynthesis genes.
source: However, several other tissues also express ecdysone biosynthesis genes (Li et al., 2022), so multiple peripheral tissues could contribute to circulating ecdysone levels.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2022.

claim: Halloween genes have very little to no expression in the fly brain based on fly brain single-cell sequencing.
source: Also, Halloween genes have very little to no expression in the fly brain based on fly brain single-cell sequencing (Davie et al., 2018), suggesting that ecdysone or 20E derives from the periphery to modulate sleep via glia.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Davie et al., 2018.

claim: Around 10–15% of cells in the Drosophila brain are glial cells belonging to one of five distinct groups.
source: In Drosophila, around 10–15% of cells in the brain are glial cells belonging to one of five distinct groups: cortex glia, astrocyte-like glia, ensheathing glia, perineurial, and subperineural glia (Edwards and Meinertzhagen, 2010; Yildirim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Edwards and Meinertzhagen, 2010 and Yildirim et al., 2019.

claim: Perineurial and subperineural glia together serve as the BBB regulating permeability, controlled by the circadian system.
source: Perineurial and subperineural glia together serve as the BBB regulating permeability, controlled by the circadian system (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: BBB glia have a role in sleep, such that endocytosis in these cells increases during sleep and depends upon the prior duration of wakefulness.
source: BBB glia also have a role in sleep, such that endocytosis in these cells increases during sleep and depends upon the prior duration of wakefulness (Artiushin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Artiushin et al., 2018.

claim: Astrocyte-like glia have a distinctive shape that allows remarkably close physical contact with synapses.
source: Astrocyte-like glia have a distinctive shape that allows remarkably close physical contact with synapses and is thought to be important for the clearance of neurotransmitters in the synaptic space (Freeman, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Freeman, 2015.

claim: Arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase 1 (AANAT1), which acetylates and inactivates monoamines, acts in astrocytes to affect sleep.
source: In support of this, arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase 1 (AANAT1), which acetylates and inactivates monoamines, acts in astrocytes to affect sleep (Davla et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Davla et al., 2020.

claim: Calcium signaling in astrocytes appears to contribute to sleep need.
source: Also, calcium signaling in astrocytes appears to contribute to sleep need (Blum et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Blum et al., 2021.

claim: Astrocytic GABA transporter maintains proper GABA tone in specific wake-promoting circadian neurons.
source: and astrocytic GABA transporter maintains proper GABA tone in specific wake-promoting circadian neurons (Chaturvedi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chaturvedi et al., 2022.

claim: Cortex glia cells encapsulate neuronal cell bodies and provide nutrients to neurons.
source: Cortex glia cells encapsulate neuronal cell bodies and provide nutrients to neurons (Doherty et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Doherty et al., 2009.

claim: Cortex and ensheathing glia accumulate most LDs in the brain.
source: Cortex and ensheathing glia accumulate most LDs in the brain, and fatty acid-binding protein (Fabp), which promotes sleep, is expressed in both glial populations (Gerstner et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gerstner et al., 2011.

claim: Ensheathing glia regulate both sleep and metabolic rate via the taurine transporter.
source: In addition, ensheathing glia regulate both sleep and metabolic rate via the taurine transporter (Stahl et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stahl et al., 2018.

claim: Roles of cortex and ensheathing glia in sleep are likely linked to their function in metabolism, which includes nutrient transfer and balance between neurons and glia.
source: Thus, roles of cortex and ensheathing glia in sleep are likely linked to their function in metabolic, which includes nutrient transfer and balance between neurons and glia (Bittern et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bittern et al., 2021.

claim: The effects of Amyloid precursor protein (App) on sleep are mediated by cortex glia.
source: We note though that the effects of Amyloid precursor protein (App), which regulates the production and deposition of toxic amyloid peptides, on sleep are mediated by cortex glia (Farca Luna et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Farca Luna et al., 2017.

claim: Ecdysone can regulate circadian rhythms through neuronally expressed receptors.
source: Additionally, while ecdysone can regulate circadian rhythms through neuronally expressed receptors (Kumar et al., 2014), we find that knockdown of glial EcRs results in more severe behavioral arrhythmicity than neuronal knockdown (Figure 2I–K).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kumar et al., 2014 and data in Figure 2I–K.

claim: Drosophila astrocytes regulate circadian locomotor rhythms.
source: As Drosophila astrocytes regulate circadian locomotor rhythms (Ng et al., 2011), they are attractive candidates for mediating the effects of ecdysone on rhythms.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ng et al., 2011.

claim: Ecdysone treatment upregulates the gene glial cell missing (gcm).
source: Ecdysone treatment upregulates the gene glial cell missing (gcm), while knockdown of EcR reduces the expression of gcm in vitro, suggesting that ecdysone influences the development and morphology of glial cells by regulating gcm, which determines the fate of the lateral glial cells (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2014.

claim: Loss of sleep alters the lipid profile across species, including in human peripheral blood.
source: Loss of sleep alters the lipid profile across species, including in human peripheral blood (Davies et al., 2014; Hinard et al., 2012; Weljie et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Davies et al., 2014; Hinard et al., 2012; Weljie et al., 2015.

claim: The lsd2 mutant and a mutant lacking a lipase affect rebound after sleep deprivation in Drosophila.
source: Conversely, lipids have been shown to regulate sleep; for instance, the lsd2 mutant we used here, as well as a mutant lacking a lipase, affect rebound after sleep deprivation in Drosophila (Thimgan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thimgan et al., 2010.

claim: Specific lipids are implicated as secreted sleep inducers (somnogens) that promote sleep following deprivation in mammals.
source: Interestingly, specific lipids are also implicated as secreted sleep inducers (somnogens) that promote sleep following deprivation in mammals (Cravatt et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cravatt et al., 1995.

claim: Sleep is associated with fat mobilization in worms, and deficits in energy mobilization in sensory neuroendocrine cells cause sleep defects.
source: Studies in worm also showed that sleep is associated with fat mobilization, and deficits in energy mobilization in sensory neuroendocrine cells cause sleep defects (Grubbs et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grubbs et al., 2020.

claim: Juvenile hormone (JH) differentially affects sleep in male and female flies.
source: Juvenile hormone (JH), which works together with ecdysone during developmental stages, differentially affects sleep in male and female flies (Leinwand and Scott, 2021; Schwedes and Carney, 2012; Wu et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Leinwand and Scott, 2021; Schwedes and Carney, 2012; Wu et al., 2018.

claim: The human ortholog of E75 is Reverb, which has broad effects on metabolism in peripheral tissues based on work in mice and humans.
source: The human ortholog of E75 is Reverb, which has broad effects on metabolism in peripheral tissues based on work in mice and humans, so the functions of EcR/E75 in peripheral tissues may also be linked to metabolism (Ding et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ding et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2017.

claim: Reverb has high expression in mouse brain glial cells.
source: In addition, Reverb has high expression in mouse brain glial cells, where it could function to affect mouse sleep (Chi-Castañeda and Ortega, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chi-Castañeda and Ortega, 2017.

claim: The endocrine system and the circuitry underlying circadian rhythms and sleep are intertwined during developmental stages.
source: In summary, the endocrine system and the circuitry underlying circadian rhythms and sleep are intertwined during developmental stages (Aldabal and Bahammam, 2011; Gamble et al., 2014; Morgan and Tsai, 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aldabal and Bahammam, 2011; Gamble et al., 2014; Morgan and Tsai, 2015.

claim: The mechanism by which ecdysone affects sleep involves LD mobilization.
source: The mechanism involves LD mobilization, emphasizing the importance of glia and lipid metabolism in sleep regulation.
evidence: This is the conclusion from the lipid droplet experiments.
